scenes.narration: What is the biggest square tile that fits this rectangle perfectly? It is eighty four units wide and thirty tall. No cutting tiles, no gaps, and every tile must be the same size, with edges aligned to the rectangle. Guess ten? It fits the height, but leaves a strip along the width. Here is a faster way. Cut off the biggest square you can: thirty by thirty. Then another. We are left with a twenty four by thirty rectangle. Any tile size that worked before must fit this leftover, because removing whole thirty unit squares removes whole rows of those tiles. And any size that tiles the leftover and the thirty unit squares also tiles the original. The common tile sizes have not changed. Turn to the leftover. Remove a twenty four by twenty four square. The thin strip is six by twenty four. Now six unit squares fill it exactly. Nothing remains. Six is the answer. Work backward: six fits twenty four, thirty, and eighty four. And no larger common tile size could have survived that final six unit strip. Reveal the grid across the whole rectangle. This is Euclid's algorithm made visible: replace the big problem with its remainder, until the remainder disappears.
